Interpretation and Its Overcoming:

Nietzsche, Active Inference, and the Organization of Experience




                          Flyxion

                          Independent Researcher


                      October 2026
ii

Preface




This book compares two bodies of work that rarely meet. One is Nietzsche’s

treatment of interpretation as a condition of organized experience that life must

nonetheless repeatedly overcome. The other is the family of theories, grouped

under predictive processing and active inference, that explain perception, action

and learning as the activity of a system maintaining an organized relation to its

surroundings. The comparison is conducted through shared problems rather than

claims of anticipation, and it keeps four kinds of claim apart:  historical claims

about what Nietzsche wrote, conceptual comparisons between his problems and

those of contemporary modelling, mathematical reconstructions that are oﬀered as

proposals, and normative arguments about which transformations of interpretation

are worth having.

   The mathematical sections are marked as reconstruction and are never pre-

sented as translation.  Literary analysis is treated as evidence about what Niet-

zsche’s writing does to a reader’s expectations, and not as an illustration of a

theory established elsewhere.

Introduction: The Organism That

Interprets




An organism that acts must treat some diﬀerences as mattering and others as

negligible. It must carry expectations about what follows from what, and it must

do so before the evidence is complete. Interpretation in this sense is a condition of

organized experience, since without a selective ordering of the ﬁeld there would be

no stable objects, no recognizable situations and no actions that could be directed

at one outcome rather than another. Yet an ordering that makes life manageable

also ﬁxes what can be noticed, and an organization adequate to one range of

circumstances can become an impediment when circumstances change or when

the organism’s own capacities outgrow it. The central problem of this book is how

interpretation can be both a condition of organized experience and something that

life must repeatedly overcome.

   Nietzsche approaches the problem through accounts of schematization, of per-

spectival knowing and of the multiplicity of drives that coordinate or contest one

another beneath the appearance of a uniﬁed subject. Predictive processing and ac-

tive inference approach a related problem from a diﬀerent direction. They explain

perception as the revision of expectations in light of discrepancy, explain action

as a means of bringing about the sensory conditions that the organism’s model

anticipates, and explain learning as the adjustment of the model that generates

those expectations (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2010; Clark, 2016; Parr et al.,

2022). Both bodies of work begin from the embodied activity of a living system

and decline to treat cognition as the inspection of a world by a detached observer.

That shared starting point is the ground of the comparison.  It does not license

the claim that either anticipated the other, and the comparison proceeds through

shared problems: how simpliﬁcation is possible without being mere distortion, how

a self is constituted as an interpretation of activity, how competing concerns ac-

quire a working hierarchy, and how an organization can be revised without being

destroyed.


                                   1

The governing thesis is stated here provisionally and defended across the chap-

ters. Nietzsche and active inference both make cognition intelligible through the

organization of an organism’s engagement with its surroundings. Nietzsche addi-

tionally asks how that organization acquires authority, and when its preservation

becomes an impediment to transformation. Active inference supplies exact vocab-

ulary for the preservation of an organization, namely the maintenance of expected

states under a generative model. It is less clear that it supplies an account of the

diﬀerence between preserving an interpretation that makes life manageable and

transforming an interpretation so that new forms of life become possible. Whether

that diﬀerence can be captured within the formalism, or whether it requires an

additional account of value, is the disagreement around which the book is orga-

nized.

   Four kinds of claim are distinguished throughout, so that resemblance at one

level never silently establishes equivalence at another. Historical claims concern

what Nietzsche wrote, in which texts, and with what changes of emphasis. Con-

ceptual comparisons concern whether a problem he poses has a counterpart in

contemporary modelling and whether the two treatments are compatible, rival

or merely parallel. Mathematical reconstructions are proposals, in which a Niet-

zschean notion is given a precise form that makes its commitments inspectable,

and each is accompanied by a statement of what it leaves out. Normative argu-

ments concern which transformations of interpretation deserve aﬃrmation, and

these are argued for on their own terms rather than read oﬀeither source.

   The method has a literary dimension that is more than ornament. Nietzsche’s

writing is aphoristic, interrupted and addressed to a reader whose expectations

it deliberately disturbs. What such writing does to a reader is evidence about

the activity of interpretation, and the book attends to it as such, asking how

transitions, changes of voice and unresolved ambiguities alter which features of a

text a reader treats as authoritative. A generic account of prediction and error

could describe some of this, but it could also ﬂatten irony, allusion and productive

ambiguity into a single quantity, and the literary chapters are written to keep that

risk visible.

   The book proceeds in ﬁve parts. The ﬁrst concerns interpretation before the

sovereign subject, taking up the textual method, the treatment of knowledge as

schematization, the ego as an interpretation of activity, and the drives as com-

peting perspectives. The second supplies the technical foundation of predictive

organization and examines action, precision and exploration. The third addresses

self-overcoming and the revision of models, including the problem of value creation.


                                   2

The fourth studies literary form as an experiment in interpretation, and the ﬁfth

extends the argument to shared models and institutions and marks the limits of

the synthesis.





                                   3

Part I


Interpretation Before the

    Sovereign Subject





                          5

Chapter 1


Reading The Will to Power as a

Problematic Archive





The textual basis of any account of Nietzschean interpretation must ﬁrst settle

what is being read. The Will to Power appeared as a book under Nietzsche’s name

only after his collapse, assembled by his associates and his sister from notebook

material of the 1880s, and the numbered aphorisms of the widely used English

edition (Nietzsche, 1967a) follow an arrangement that Nietzsche did not give them.

The critical edition prepared by Colli and Montinari restored the notebooks to

their chronological order and made it possible to see that the plan of a systematic

work under this title was entertained, revised and eventually abandoned in 1888,

when Nietzsche turned instead to the writings he completed (Montinari, 1982). A

passage quoted from the compilation therefore comes with two kinds of uncertainty.

It may record a thought that was later developed, tested against objections and

published in a ﬁnished work, or it may record a trial formulation that Nietzsche

dropped.

   The method adopted here follows from that situation. Passages from the note-

books are used to reconstruct a constellation of problems and are never treated

as articles of a ﬁnished doctrine. Where a claim about interpretation appears in

the compilation, it is located in its notebook context where that can be done, and

compared with its treatment in The Gay Science, Beyond Good and Evil, On the

Genealogy of Morality and Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Nietzsche, 1974, 1966, 1967b,

2006). Agreement between the notebooks and a published work strengthens an

attribution. Disagreement is recorded as a tension or as a change of emphasis, and

is not smoothed away to produce a uniﬁed position. Systematic readings of Niet-

zsche exist and are argued with care (Richardson, 1996), and the present method


                                   7

does not exclude them. It requires only that any systematic reading say which of

its premises rest on published statements and which on material Nietzsche chose

not to publish.

   The comparison can be made concrete for the doctrine of the next chapter. The

notebook claim that knowing is a schematizing that imposes regularity as far as

practical needs require (section 515 of the compilation) has published counterparts

of diﬀerent weight.  Section 24 of Beyond Good and Evil describes cognition as

a will to simpliﬁcation that has contrived to preserve ignorance in the service

of life, and section 354 of The Gay Science derives conscious thought from the

pressure of communication, so that what reaches awareness is already shaped by

what can be shared. Both passages support the notebook’s picture of cognition

as practical simpliﬁcation, and neither states it as a general theory of knowledge

in the compilation’s terms. The attribution adopted below is accordingly that

Nietzsche held the schematizing thesis as a recurring problem and not that he

ﬁxed it as a doctrine, and the dating and notebook identiﬁers of the relevant

entries in the critical edition remain to be supplied wherever a claim rests on the

compilation alone.

  A literary question enters at the outset and recurs throughout the book. Apho-

ristic and experimental writing, when reorganized into the form of a philosophical

system, acquires expectations of continuity, hierarchy and doctrinal consistency

that the original writing did not claim to satisfy. A reader who meets numbered

sections arranged under headings on knowledge, nature, society and art will tend

to assume that earlier sections ground later ones and that apparent contradictions

are failures of exposition. The editorial arrangement thus supplies an interpretive

frame before any sentence is read. This is itself an instance of the phenomenon

under study, since an organization imposed on material determines which relations

among its parts are visible, which are salient and which are treated as noise. The

material form of Nietzsche’s reception is accordingly part of the argument about

how interpretation organizes its objects, and the reading practice adopted in later

chapters aims to resist the frame without pretending to a neutral standpoint out-

side any frame.





                                   8

Chapter 2


Knowledge as Schematization





Nietzsche’s treatments of identity, regularity and the concept share a recurring

claim: that the cognition which makes a stable world available does so by treating

unlike things as like and by imposing regularity on a ﬂux that does not present itself

in that form. The notebooks put this in terms of schematization, an activity that,

as section 515 of the compilation has it, imposes upon chaos as much regularity

and form as practical needs require. The question this chapter pursues is whether

such activity should be described as the discovery of an order or as the making

of experience tractable through an ordering. The two descriptions diﬀer in what

they permit one to say about error. If cognition discovers order, a schema is false

to the degree that it fails to match what is there.  If cognition makes experience

tractable, a schema may be adequate or inadequate relative to a task, a scale and

a form of life, and the word error needs a diﬀerent home.

   The question of error is sharper than it ﬁrst appears. A useful simpliﬁcation

does not become false merely because it suppresses diﬀerences, since every concept

suppresses some. What matters is whether the suppressed diﬀerences are idle

with respect to the purposes the concept serves. The same simpliﬁcation can be

adequate for one purpose and ruinous for another, and it can pass from the ﬁrst

condition to the second when circumstances change. A reading of Nietzsche on

which all schematization is equally falsifying cannot make this distinction, and a

reading on which it is simply true cannot explain why he treats the same schemata

as both indispensable and as objects of suspicion.

   Coarse-graining supplies a precise vocabulary for the point. Let X be a detailed

state space and let an interpretive organization be a map


                         ϕ : X −→Z,


                                   9

where Z contains the distinctions available to the organism. Because distinct states

of X may be sent to the same state of Z, the organization necessarily discards

diﬀerences. The relevant question is which discarded diﬀerences remain irrelevant

to action and which later become consequential. This can be made exact relative

to a task.


Deﬁnition 2.1 (Task-relative suﬃciency). Let T be a task speciﬁed by a class

of admissible policies and a loss ℓdeﬁned on X. An organization ϕ : X →Z is

ε-suﬃcient for T if the best expected loss attainable by policies that depend on X

only through ϕ exceeds the best expected loss attainable by policies that depend

on X directly by no more than ε.


   The deﬁnition gives sense to the claim that an organization is adequate without

being a copy. It also makes adequacy fragile in the way the notebooks suggest. If

the task changes, or if the distribution of encountered states shifts, a map that

was ε-suﬃcient for the earlier task and distribution may cease to be so, although

nothing about the map itself has altered. A simpliﬁcation can thus pass from

harmless to harmful through a change in what the organism does or where it lives.

This gives a precise reading of the claim that errors of cognition are conditions of

life: the simpliﬁcation is a condition of life for the tasks it serves, and an error for

those it does not.

Remark 2.1. The deﬁnition does not say that all schematization is innocent. It says

that the evaluation of a schema requires a speciﬁcation of task and environment,

and that the speciﬁcation can itself be contested. A reconstruction of Nietzsche’s

view that left this contestation out would explain only the half of his position on

which schemata are useful.





                                   10

Chapter 3


The Ego as an Interpretation of

Activity





Nietzsche’s criticism of a substantial subject, a simple inner proprietor who thinks,

wills and owns its acts, is often taken to imply a denial of agency. The two should

be kept apart. The disappearance of a simple proprietor leaves the fact of orga-

nized action in place, together with the need to explain how a plurality of processes

acquires enough coordination to act, to remember, to promise and to experience it-

self as continuous. The explanatory task is thereby changed rather than abolished.

Instead of asking what the self is, one asks how a self-describing coordination is

produced and maintained, and what its description leaves out. Nietzsche’s own

positive proposal, in Beyond Good and Evil, section 12, is to understand the soul

as a multiplicity, a social structure of drives and aﬀects, and section 19 analy-

ses willing as a relation of commanding and obeying within the one who wills.

The feeling of being a uniﬁed agent can conceal the complex activity that pro-

duces it, since the one who commands identiﬁes with the commanding side and

takes credit for what the whole organization accomplishes. The ego is accordingly

partly an achievement of organization and partly a misleading interpretation of

that achievement.

   The comparison with contemporary modelling concerns the distinction between

a process and its representation of its own activity. A system may maintain a

model that summarizes its bodily states, its action possibilities and the expected

consequences of acting, without that model transparently disclosing the mecha-

nisms that generate the behaviour it summarizes. Such a self-model is useful in

the way schemata are useful:  it compresses a large and partly inaccessible set of

processes into a form that can guide planning and be communicated to others.


                                   11

It can also mislead in a systematic way. A model that presents the system as

a uniﬁed deliberator will explain actions by appeal to decisions and will render

the contest of concerns that produced them invisible, which is the pattern that

Nietzsche diagnoses in the ordinary grammar of willing.

   The easy conclusion, that an interpreted self is therefore unreal, does not

follow and should be resisted. An interpretation can have causal consequences. It

can regulate conduct, structure what the organism attends to, shape what others

expect of it, and become an object of investment, so that challenges to it are felt as

challenges to the organism and not merely to a proposition. These eﬀects obtain

even when the interpretation’s account of its own origins is mistaken. The self so

understood is neither a substance nor an illusion in the sense of a mere appearance

without eﬀect.  It is an organization that has consequences, and the questions it

raises are about its authority, its revisability and the cost of revising it, which

later chapters take up.

   The distinction between an agent and the model an agent has of itself also bears

on the relation between responsibility and metaphysics. Promising and being held

to a promise require that conduct be coordinated across time, and a self-model

that supports such coordination is practically necessary whatever its metaphysical

standing. The Nietzschean question is therefore what kind of coordination a given

self-interpretation makes possible and what kinds it forecloses, and this question

can be asked without settling whether any inner proprietor exists.





                                   12

Chapter 4


Drives, Perspectives, and

Competing Interpretations




The term drive is used by Nietzsche in ways that resist a single analysis. Sometimes

it names an impulse that presses for discharge, sometimes an evaluative orientation

that gives things their signiﬁcance, sometimes a competing organization that seeks

to interpret the whole in its own terms. These senses are not obviously consistent,

and the comparative problem is sharpened by a diﬀerence of method. Many active-

inference models begin with a speciﬁed agent and a speciﬁed objective, and ask how

the agent should perceive and act. Nietzsche frequently makes the organization of

the agent itself a site of conﬂict, so that the question of whose objective governs

is open and its answer can change.

  A  reconstruction can  represent  partially competing  evaluative  processes

through objectives Fi, each of which assesses states and policies from its own

standpoint, and an eﬀective organization such as

           ∑
                           Feﬀ(s) =    wi(s) Fi(s).

                                                                      i

Proposal 4.1. Treat a Nietzschean multiplicity as a family of objectives {Fi}

together with state-dependent weights wi(s) that determine which concerns govern

conduct in which situations.


   What matters philosophically is the weights and not the sum. The sum rep-

resents a momentary settlement, whereas the weights encode a hierarchy, and the

question that Nietzsche presses is what determines which concerns dominate and

how that determination can change. If the weights are ﬁxed, the multiplicity col-

lapses into a single objective with a complicated shape, and nothing distinctively


                                   13

Nietzschean remains.  If the weights depend on state, they can shift as circum-

stances shift, which captures the idea that a drive may dominate in one setting

and be subordinate in another.  If they depend on the history of the organism, a

further structure is needed to describe how hierarchies are acquired, and this is

where an account of formation and revision becomes necessary.

    It is important to say what this proposal does not claim.  It does not trans-

late drives into computational modules, and it does not suggest that Nietzsche

had a weighted sum in mind.  It oﬀers a form that makes certain commitments

inspectable, and one of its uses is to reveal where the form fails. When the objec-

tives Fi are not commensurable, so that no common scale licenses adding them,

the scalar Feﬀis an artefact of the reconstruction and not a feature of the phe-

nomenon. In such cases the conﬂict is better represented as an ordering that is

partial, or as a contest whose resolution is a matter of the organization taking

one form rather than another. Part of the later discussion of value creation turns

on whether a framework that begins from a scalar objective can represent such

conﬂicts without silently reintroducing an evaluator that stands above them.

Part II


Predictive Organization and

     Interested Action





                            15

Chapter 5


Predictive Coding, Active

Inference, and the Limits of

Analogy





The comparison pursued in this book depends on a technical vocabulary whose

terms are often run together, and the ﬁrst task is to keep them apart. Predictive

coding names a family of schemes in which a processing hierarchy transmits pre-

dictions downward and discrepancies upward, so that what propagates through

the system is chieﬂy the part of the input that the current prediction fails to

account for (Rao and Ballard, 1999). Bayesian inference names a normative rela-

tion between prior beliefs, a likelihood and a posterior, and says nothing about

how a physical system might realize it. Variational inference is an approximation

technique for cases in which the exact posterior is intractable, and it proceeds by

choosing a tractable family of distributions and selecting the member closest to

the posterior. Active inference extends this apparatus by treating action and pol-

icy selection as further consequences of the same optimization, so that an agent is

described as selecting the courses of action under which its expected observations

accord with a generative model that includes preferred outcomes (Friston et al.,

2017; Parr et al., 2022). The free-energy principle is the broadest of these claims, a

proposal about the conditions under which any self-organizing system that persists

can be described as if it were performing such inference (Friston, 2010). Each step

in this sequence adds assumptions, and a conclusion licensed at one step is not

licensed at the next. These terms are kept separate throughout, and a comparison

with Nietzsche that depends on the stronger claims will say so.

   The central mathematical object is the variational free energy. For a generative


                                   17

model p(o, s) over observations o and hidden states s, and an approximate posterior

q(s), it is deﬁned by


       F[q; o] = Eq(s)[log q(s) −log p(o, s)] = DKL(q(s) ∥p(s | o)) −log p(o).


The second equality follows from the factorization p(o, s) = p(s | o) p(o), which

allows the logarithm of the joint to be split into a term that depends on s and a

term that does not. Two consequences are immediate. Because the divergence is

non-negative, F is an upper bound on the surprise −log p(o), with equality exactly

when q equals the exact posterior. And because log p(o) does not depend on q,

minimizing F over q is the same as minimizing the divergence between q and the

posterior, so that perception, understood as the choice of q, becomes approximate

Bayesian inference.

    It is equally important to say what does not follow. Minimizing F under a

given generative model yields a posterior that is best relative to that model.  It

carries no guarantee that the model is adequate, that its state space contains

the distinctions the situation requires, or that its priors deserve the conﬁdence

they receive. The bound on surprise is a bound on surprise as assessed by the

model, so that an agent whose model is poor can drive F low by attending to

what the model handles well. Approximate inference under a generative model

does not by itself establish a philosophical perspectivism, an ontology of power or

a criterion of ﬂourishing. Where active inference is invoked in later chapters, it is

invoked for what the formalism actually delivers, and the gap between that and

the Nietzschean questions about authority and transformation is itself part of the

subject.

   Action enters through the expected free energy of a policy π. In one common

formulation,


             G(π) = DKL(q(o | π) ∥p(o)) + Eq(s|π)[H[p(o | s)]] ,


where the ﬁrst term measures the divergence between predicted and preferred out-

comes, often called risk, and the second measures the expected ambiguity of the

mapping from states to observations. Policies with low G are those expected to

bring about preferred outcomes through observations that are informative about

hidden states, and the decomposition of Appendix B shows that this informative-

ness is the expected information gain. The preferred outcomes are encoded in p(o),

which is part of the model and not derived from the formalism. This observation


                                   18

is of ﬁrst importance for what follows, since the authority of those preferences is

exactly what the Nietzschean question about value presses on, and Chapter 12

returns to it.





                                  19

Chapter 6


Action as the Transformation of

Evidence





An organism does not receive evidence passively. What it encounters depends on

where it goes, what it handles, whom it asks and what it ignores, and each of these

is in turn shaped by the interpretation it already holds. Perception and action

are therefore mutually implicated in a strong sense.  Action determines which

observations occur, which uncertainties can be resolved and which expectations

meet repeated conﬁrmation, and the resulting observations determine how the

interpretation is revised. In the formal setting this appears as the dependence of

the observation distribution on the policy, written q(o | π), so that the evidence

available for assessing a model is partly a product of the model’s own use.

   The Nietzschean comparison becomes especially productive at this point. An

interpretation can organize practices that make its world increasingly familiar and

manageable. A way of reading situations leads to a way of acting in them, the

acting produces situations of the kind the reading handles well, and the reading

appears to be conﬁrmed. This is the problem of endogenous evidence: apparent

conﬁrmation may result partly from restricting encounters to situations that an

existing model already handles well. A record of success is evidence about an in-

terpretation only to the extent that the encounters composing it were not selected

by the interpretation to ensure that success.

   Three kinds of action should be distinguished, because they stand in diﬀerent

relations to the evidential standing of the interpretation they serve. Successful in-

tervention is action that changes a situation in the way the interpretation predicts,

and where the situation was not chosen to guarantee that result, it counts as a

genuine test that the interpretation passed. Selective exposure is the arrangement


                                   21

of one’s circumstances so that only situations of a manageable kind arise, and

the conﬁrmations it produces are largely manufactured. Exploratory action seeks

situations in which the interpretation’s predictions are uncertain or likely to fail,

and its results bear on the interpretation in proportion to that risk. The same

observable pattern, a long run of conﬁrmed predictions, can arise from any of the

three, and nothing in the record of conﬁrmations alone distinguishes them.

   The distinction can be given a simple form. Let µπ be the distribution over

situations that an agent following policy π actually encounters, and let ν be a

reference distribution over the situations that matter for the agent’s continued

viability, which may include situations it rarely meets. Write ℓ(x) for the model’s

expected prediction error in situation x.


Deﬁnition 6.1 (Insulation gap). The insulation gap of a policy π for a model

with error proﬁle ℓis


                   ∆(π) = Ex∼ν[ℓ(x)] −Ex∼µπ[ℓ(x)] .


  A large positive gap indicates that the model performs far better on the situ-

ations its policy leads it to meet than on those that matter for its viability. This

is the signature of selective exposure, but it is equally the signature of eﬀective

specialization or of successful environmental management, in which an agent le-

gitimately transforms its surroundings so that the model’s competence suﬃces.

The gap measures a disparity in performance relative to a speciﬁed reference dis-

tribution and does not identify its cause, which requires further evidence about

how the encountered situations came to be selected. A gap near zero shows only

that the average error is the same under the two distributions. It does not show

that the distributions coincide, since very diﬀerent distributions can yield equal

expected values of a single loss. The reference distribution ν cannot be read oﬀ

the formalism, and its speciﬁcation is a substantive and contestable choice. This

is the point at which the formal reconstruction acknowledges its dependence on

something outside itself, since which situations matter for the agent’s continuation

is a question about the agent’s form of life, and Chapter 17 argues that it must be

answered by an account of correction that the formalism does not by itself supply.

   The notion also clariﬁes why defensive coherence is not obviously a failure from

within. An agent that has arranged its circumstances so that its interpretation is

never seriously challenged will report low error, high conﬁdence and a sense that

its view of the world is well supported. Only a comparison with situations it does

not meet reveals the gap, and an agent organized to avoid such situations has little


                                   22

occasion to make the comparison.





                                  23

Chapter 7


Precision, Attention, and the

Authority of an Interpretation




In predictive models the inﬂuence of a discrepancy depends on how it is weighted.

A large error that is assigned low precision barely alters the system’s estimates,

whereas a small error assigned high precision can drive large revisions. Precision

is thereby a mechanism of attention and of authority:  it determines which dis-

crepancies are heard. In a Nietzschean register the corresponding point is that an

encounter does not arrive with an unquestionable authority independent of the

organization receiving it. Whether a surprising event counts as a refutation, an

anomaly, a nuisance or an opportunity depends on how the interpretation that

meets it is disposed to weigh it. Some discrepancies become transformative while

others are dismissed, subordinated or redescribed, and the diﬀerence lies largely

in the weighting.

  A local quadratic approximation makes the structure explicit. For a prediction

error ε and a precision matrix Π, the weighted discrepancy is


                            E = 1 εTΠ ε.                                                2


In a Gaussian model with observation noise precision Π, the negative log-likelihood

of an observation has the form


               −log p(o | s) = 1 εTΠ ε −1 log|Π| + const,                                           2           2


where ε is the diﬀerence between the observation and its prediction. The second

term deserves attention. It shows that discounting an error by lowering precision

is not free within the formalism, since the log-determinant term penalizes low pre-


                                   25

cision and so charges for any claim that the observations are generally unreliable.

A model that could silence every discrepancy by setting Π close to zero would be

penalized for implying that its own observations carry almost no information. The

formalism thus builds in a limited resistance to wholesale insulation, although it

cannot prevent a model from raising precision on conﬁrming channels and lowering

it on disconﬁrming ones at a modest total cost.

   The philosophical question therefore concerns the formation and revision of

Π more than the elimination of ε. An account that treats precision as a given

parameter to be estimated leaves open who or what assigns authority to some

channels of evidence over others, and how that assignment itself becomes open to

challenge. If precision is learned from the history of past reliability, then an agent

whose history was shaped by selective exposure will have learned precisions that

reﬂect its insulation, and the learning process reproduces rather than corrects the

bias of Chapter 6. Revising precision in the face of a discrepancy that the current

precision already discounts is thus a distinctive diﬃculty, and it is one that the

literary chapters later examine as a problem of how a text can alter what a reader

takes to be authoritative.

   This connects the technical notion to reading.  Transitions, interruptions,

changes of voice and shifts in aﬀect can be studied as ways of altering which

Chapter 10


Defensive Coherence and

Interpretive Entrapment





An interpretation can maintain its coherence by reducing its exposure to correction.

The mechanisms are familiar from the preceding chapters: selective attention that

assigns low precision to disconﬁrming channels, constrained action that avoids

situations where the interpretation is at risk, reinterpretation of counterexamples

so that they conﬁrm what they appeared to challenge, and dependence on social

environments that reward repetition of the received view. A system organized in

this way can become increasingly eﬀective at preserving its interpretation while

becoming less capable of handling changes beyond the protected domain.  Its

reported coherence improves as its adequacy to the wider situation declines.

    Nietzsche’s analysis of the ascetic ideal supplies an unusually rich case.  In

the third essay of On the Genealogy of Morality, especially in sections 7 and 8,

the philosopher’s withdrawal from ordinary pleasures and obligations is presented

as serving the conditions of intellectual work, so that renunciation can express

a powerful commitment to a task. The broader ascetic ideal, however, can turn

suﬀering into an indictment of earthly existence and make detachment a doctrine

about life as such. Outwardly similar acts of detachment can accordingly serve

very diﬀerent dispositions: one a discipline that enables activity, the other a de-

fence that forecloses it. The concluding section of the essay presses the point

further by observing that human beings would sooner will nothingness than not

will. An apparent escape from attachment can preserve an attachment to purity,

to salvation or to the identity of one who has transcended ordinary needs. The

will has changed its object, and perhaps turned against itself, without ceasing.

On the reading developed here, this is a precise instance of defensive coherence:

object it cannot give up.

not amount to an unchanged evaluator that ranks every transformation, and mu-

Chapter 15


Metaphor, Concept Formation,

and the Invention of Distinctions





Metaphor is a possible means of reorganizing salience and conceptual structure,

and Nietzsche gives it a foundational role. In the early essay “On Truth and Lies

in a Nonmoral Sense,” which he did not publish (Nietzsche, 1979), concepts are

described as the residue of metaphors whose ﬁgurative origin has been forgotten,

so that what passes for literal truth is the accumulated and worn-out product

of transfers between spheres. Whatever one makes of the historical claim about

language, the thought has a systematic consequence for the framework of this book.

Schematization, in the sense of Chapter 2, requires a stock of distinctions, and the

origin of new distinctions is the question that Chapter 9 left open. Metaphor is

one candidate for where some of them come from.

   Two functions can be distinguished. Some metaphors help a reader assimilate

an unfamiliar subject to an existing category, so that the unfamiliar is handled

by the repertoire already in place. Others make previously unnoticed relations

available for thought, so that something is seen as having a structure it was not

seen to have.  Only the second function bears on structural revision. A way

of stating the diﬀerence is that assimilating metaphors act within the current

representation, whereas generative metaphors alter it.

   The mathematical discussion returns to representation maps. Let ϕ : X →Z
be the existing organization and let a candidate representation be ϕ′  : X →Z′.
Three relations between them correspond to three eﬀects.  If ϕ = g ◦ϕ′ for some

map g, the new representation reﬁnes the old one and introduces distinctions that
the old one lacked.  If ϕ′ = g ◦ϕ, it coarsens it and renders earlier distinctions

dispensable. If neither holds, the two cut the state space along incomparable lines,


                                   53

and the new representation both preserves some distinctions and loses others. A

metaphor can be modelled as a partial structure-preserving map h from a source

domain with relations RS to a target domain, proposing the relations h(RS) as

new relations on the target. Whether the proposal is productive is then assessed

by the criterion of Chapter 2: whether the representation it induces is suﬃcient,

to within an acceptable margin, for the tasks that matter, and whether it opens

tasks that the previous one could not formulate.

   Model selection and minimum description length supply a second comparison.

A description length criterion prefers the representation minimizing the sum of

the length of the model and the length of the data given the model, in the manner

of Rissanen’s principle (Rissanen, 1978). Such criteria capture a real virtue, the

compression of regularities, and they might be expected to favour metaphors that

unify disparate phenomena.  Neither shorter descriptions nor greater predictive

accuracy is assumed here to exhaust literary or philosophical value. A metaphor

may lengthen the description of the data in the short term, since it introduces a

structure whose payoﬀarrives only later or in another domain, and a metaphor’s

worth can lie in the questions it makes askable and not in the accuracy of its

answers. The criteria also assume that the data to be described are given, whereas

a generative metaphor can alter what counts as data.

   The chapter therefore asks how a text can expand interpretive possibilities

without immediately settling them. A metaphor that settles its relation to the

target at once becomes a deﬁnition and loses its generative force, whereas one

that leaves the transferred structure partly open invites the reader to continue

the mapping. This returns the argument to the reader. The transformation of

the reader’s repertoire is accomplished through the reader’s own work with the

ﬁgure, and to that extent the text enacts the claim of Chapter 9 that new distinc-

tions are not obtained by inference within a ﬁxed family but made available to it.

Whether such availability can be assessed by any standard other than the reader’s

subsequent capacities is a question that the ﬁnal part carries into the discussion

of shared models and institutions.

Chapter 16


Shared Models, Institutions, and

Collective Self-Conﬁrmation




The argument so far has treated interpretation as the achievement of an individ-

ual organism, but the organization of experience is largely inherited and socially

maintained. Language supplies the distinctions that a person can draw before any

inquiry begins. Education trains attention and ﬁxes which discrepancies a learner

is taught to notice.  Scientiﬁc instruments, record-keeping practices, habits and

institutions determine what can be encountered at all and what can be recognized

as evidence when it is. A model that an individual holds is therefore frequently a

local instance of a model that a community maintains, and the questions of the

earlier chapters, about insulation, precision and revisability, recur at the collective

scale with their own mechanisms.

   The formal treatment introduces coupled agents i = 1, . . . , n with distinct

observations, models and preferences, who exchange reports and inﬂuence one
another’s updates. The simplest tractable case is linear averaging. Let xt ∈Rn

collect the agents’ current estimates of a quantity and let W be a row-stochastic

matrix recording how much weight each agent places on each other’s estimate, so

that

                                  xt+1 = Wxt.

When the network is connected and aperiodic, the estimates converge to a con-
sensus, and the consensus value is πTx0, where π is the left eigenvector of W for

eigenvalue one, normalized to sum to one. The weights πi measure the long-run

inﬂuence of each agent’s initial estimate. Agreement is thus guaranteed by the

structure of the coupling, but its content depends on who holds inﬂuence. Golub

and Jackson showed that if initial estimates are independent noisy signals of a


                                   57

truth, the consensus converges to the truth as the group grows only if no agent

retains non-vanishing inﬂuence (Golub and Jackson, 2010). Where one authority

is heavily weighted, the group converges just as ﬁrmly, and converges on that

authority’s initial error.

   Agreement can arise in several ways that the observation of agreement alone

does not distinguish.  It can arise from shared evidence, in which case the con-

vergence is justiﬁed to the extent that the evidence is good.  It can arise from

dependence on a common authority, in which case a single source is counted many

times.  It can arise from coordinated inquiry in which agents test one another’s

claims against independent encounters. And it can arise from the suppression of

dissent, in which disagreement is removed from the data of the system and not

resolved. The double-counting case admits a simple statement. Suppose that n

agents each form a log-odds estimate ℓfor a hypothesis from one and the same

signal, and that a naive pooling procedure sums the reports as though they were

independent. The pooled value is nℓ, although the evidence supports only ℓ, so

that apparent conﬁdence grows with the number of agents while the information

stays ﬁxed. A community in which agents cite one another, each citing in turn

the same source, displays exactly this structure.

   The notion of insulation introduced in Chapter 6 carries over. Let µ denote

the distribution over situations that a community’s institutional practices lead it

to encounter, and ν the distribution over situations that matter for its continued

viability. A large gap between the error the community’s model makes on ν and on

µ is compatible with collective selective exposure, a self-conﬁrming arrangement in

which instruments, categories and incentives combine to supply only the evidence

the model already handles. Like its individual counterpart, the gap may instead

reﬂect legitimate specialization, and which reading is correct requires evidence

about how the encountered situations were selected. Where the arrangement is

one of self-conﬁrmation, because it is distributed, no individual need intend it, and

no individual may be in a position to see it. The chapter accordingly examines the

conditions under which collective convergence improves knowledge and those under

which it merely stabilizes a shared error. Convergence improves knowledge when

the sources feeding it are independent, when inﬂuence is not concentrated, and

when disagreement can enter the record. It stabilizes error when these conditions

fail, and from inside the community the two cases may look alike.

Chapter 17


Power, Truth, and the

Availability of Correction




A perspectival account of knowledge faces an obvious objection. If every interpre-

tation is a perspective shaped by interests and capacities, there seems to be no

ground for distinguishing stronger inquiry from eﬀective self-insulation, since both

are ways of organizing experience in the service of an organization’s persistence.

This chapter proposes a criterion and argues for it. The criterion concerns an

interpretation’s ability to sustain consequential encounters with what it does not

already accommodate. Such a criterion requires argument, and it is not presented

as an automatic consequence of either Nietzsche or active inference.

    Nietzsche supplies a resource in the third essay of the Genealogy, where he

rejects a view from nowhere and claims that the more aﬀects are allowed to speak

about a thing, and the more diﬀerent eyes can be brought to observe  it, the

more complete the concept of that thing, and the objectivity attainable, will be.

Perspectivism in this form is a claim about the conditions of better knowing:

knowledge improves with the number and diﬀerence of the perspectives brought

to bear and not through escape from perspective. The remark already points

toward the institutional dimension of the present chapter, since a plurality of

perspectives has to be housed somewhere and its challenges have to be able to

reach the organization they challenge.

   The discussion connects epistemic authority to the practical availability of cor-

rection, and the following deﬁnition states the three conditions that the criterion

involves.


Deﬁnition 17.1 (Correctability). An organization is correctable with respect to

a class of challenges C if, for each c ∈C, (i) the challenge can be registered by the


                                   59

organization at a precision that is not negligible, (ii) the cost borne by the party

raising it is bounded and does not exceed what that party can reasonably sustain,

and (iii) a revision in response to the challenge does not destroy the conditions of

the organization’s own activity.


   Each condition names a way correction fails. The ﬁrst fails when precision

on the relevant channel has been driven to zero by the mechanisms of Chapter 7,

so that the challenge is received and not heard. The second fails when raising a

challenge exposes the challenger to penalties severe enough that challenges are not

raised, which makes the record of dissent a poor guide to the existence of grounds

for it. The third fails when the organization cannot revise without collapse, so that

even a challenge heard and welcomed cannot be acted on, and it is the condition

through which the problem of transition cost from Chapter 9 enters. Who can

challenge a model, what costs do they bear, and can the organization receiving

the challenge change without destroying the conditions of its own activity are, in

this formulation, three questions with three distinct answers.

   This  gives the monograph an  institutional dimension and prevents  self-

overcoming from remaining an exclusively heroic individual achievement. The

supports discussed in Chapter 11 for a person reappear as the arrangements

through which a community can hear and absorb correction:  procedures for

adversarial testing, protected channels for dissent, redundancy of independent

sources, and structures that spread the cost of revision. Where such arrangements

exist, a community can transform itself without the intervention of an exceptional

individual.  Where they are absent, a community depends on the rare person

willing to bear the full cost of challenge, and the conditions of the third kind

make it likely that even then nothing changes.

   The criterion should not be mistaken for a theory of truth, and it carries a

limit that the ﬁnal chapter records.  It identiﬁes the availability of correction

as a mark of an inquiry that is capable of becoming better, and it is silent on

whether the direction of change is an enhancement. An organization can be highly

correctable and be corrected toward a worse condition by challenges that are

themselves illusory. The criterion thus discriminates between self-insulating and

self-revising organizations, which is what the perspectival account needed, without

deciding which revisions deserve aﬃrmation.

Chapter 18


The Limits of the Synthesis




A comparison should state where it ceases to hold. The preceding chapters identi-

ﬁed several points of real contact between Nietzsche’s treatment of interpretation

and the active-inference family of models. Schematization corresponds to coarse-

graining relative to a task, with the diﬀerence that the formal notion is exact

about what is lost. The ego as an interpretation of activity corresponds to a

self-model that summarizes an organism’s processes without disclosing them. The

dependence of an error’s inﬂuence on its weighting corresponds to precision, and

the dependence of evidence on what the organism does corresponds to the policy-

dependence of observations. Each of these correspondences is a resemblance of

problem, supported by a formal construction, and each was advanced with a state-

ment of what it leaves out.

   Three limits deserve ﬁnal statement. The ﬁrst is whether will to power can

be represented through a scalar objective. The argument of Chapter 4 showed

that a weighted sum of objectives is a coherent form only where the objectives

are commensurable, and Chapter 12 argued that the will to power functions in

Nietzsche’s use as an organizing activity within which preferences are formed, and

not as a preference of high weight.   If so, the attempt to identify it with the

quantity minimized in active inference, or with any single information-theoretic

measure, mistakes the category of the notion. The second limit concerns evaluative

conﬂicts, which may not admit a common measure at all. Where the conﬂict is

between ways of life and not between values on a shared scale, the formalism’s

tools of weighting and tradeoﬀpresuppose what is in dispute. The third limit is

whether literary transformation can be captured by changes in a generative model.

Chapters 13 to 15 found that the predictive vocabulary describes some of what a

text does to a reader, namely the shifting of expectation and the reallocation of

attention, but that it needs added structure to represent irony and allusion, and


                                   61

that it oﬀers no way of separating productive plurality from idle uncertainty or of

saying why one disruption illuminates while another merely disorients.

  A distinction runs through all three limits and should be kept explicit in the

conclusion.  Empirical questions about cognitive mechanisms, such as whether

perception is implemented by hierarchical prediction, are answered by evidence

about organisms, and the formal tools may prove accurate or inaccurate as models

of them. Philosophical judgments about which forms of life deserve aﬃrmation

are questions of a diﬀerent kind, and no result about mechanism settles them. The

syntheses most likely to mislead are those that present a ﬁnding of the ﬁrst kind

as though it carried a verdict of the second, or that borrow the authority of a

mathematical result for a valuation that the mathematics does not contain.

   The conclusion that the book defends preserves a productive asymmetry. Ac-

tive inference oﬀers formal tools for understanding perception, action, learning

and exploration, and it supplies exact vocabulary for what it is to preserve an

organization and to revise a model within a family. Nietzsche presses questions

about the authority and transformation of the organizations those tools describe,

in particular how a family of models or a hierarchy of preferences acquires its

standing and what it would be to replace it. The conjunction is most useful when

each exposes questions left open by the other. From the formal side, the open

questions are the origin of structural novelty and the authority of the objective.

From Nietzsche’s side, they are the conditions under which self-overcoming can

be sustained and the standards by which its results are to be judged, and the

chapters on attachment, institutions and correctability suggest that part of the

answer lies in the relations and arrangements that make revision bearable.

   The question posed at the outset was how an organism can remain suﬃciently

organized to act while retaining the capacity to revise the interpretations through

which action becomes possible. The answer developed here is conditional and in

part negative. The capacity to revise depends on exposure that is not engineered

to conﬁrm, on weights that can themselves be challenged, on supports that dis-

tribute the cost of transformation, and on access to alternatives that lie outside

the family currently in use, which optimization within that family does not itself

explain. Undergoing such revision may therefore require more than accepting a

better proposition. It may require changes in attention, aﬀect, identiﬁcation and

the reader’s relation to authority, which is why a book about interpretation had

to attend to how its principal author writes, and not only to what he says.

Since p(o, s) = p(s | o) p(o), the logarithm of the joint splits as log p(s | o)+log p(o).

Substituting, and noting that log p(o) does not depend on s,


 F[q; o] = Eq(s)[log q(s) −log p(s | o)] −log p(o) = DKL(q(s) ∥p(s | o)) −log p(o).

Appendix C


Coarse-Graining and

Task-Relative Suﬃciency




Recall the deﬁnition of Chapter 2. For a task T with loss ℓ(a, x) over actions a
and states x ∈X, and a distribution over X, let RX denote the least expected loss

over policies that may depend on x, and let Rϕ denote the least expected loss over

policies that depend on x only through ϕ(x). The organization ϕ is ε-suﬃcient
for T  if Rϕ −RX ≤ε.  Since policies depending on ϕ(x) are a subset of those
depending on x, Rϕ ≥RX always.

Proposal C.1. If the loss depends on x only through ϕ(x), that is ℓ(a, x) =
˜ℓ(a, ϕ(x)) for some ˜ℓ, then ϕ is 0-suﬃcient.

Proof. Take any policy πX depending on x. For each value z in the range of ϕ,
the loss is constant across the ﬁbre ϕ−1(z) for any ﬁxed action, so the expected

loss of πX is a mixture of ﬁbre-wise losses and is minimized by choosing in each
ﬁbre the action that minimizes ˜ℓ(·, z) averaged over the within-ﬁbre distribution

of πX’s choices. That action depends on x only through z = ϕ(x), so a policy

depending only on ϕ(x) attains the same minimum.

coordinates (a, b) and let ϕ(a, b) = a. For a task whose loss is (u −a)2, where
